roles.title: Risk manager (CRO)
roles.who: Who runs the risk management process.

tasks.text: Keep the taxonomy, appetite and impact criteria of each company
Check on the dashboard the risks outside appetite, the quality suggestions and the treatment effectiveness
Review the staff reports and turn them into events or risks
Take the quarterly snapshot and present the Board report
Keep the methodology up to date and share it

roles.when: Weekly: dashboard and reports received. Quarterly: snapshot and report. Yearly: appetite and methodology.

roles.title: Risk owner
roles.who: Managers accountable for a process and its risks.

tasks.text: Register the risks of your area with the wizard or the library
Keep the assessment up to date and follow the quality suggestions
Define the treatment plan: actions, responsibles and due dates
Record the loss events that happen in your area
Review each risk at least once a year and record the review

roles.when: When an e-mail alert arrives, and at least once a quarter in My ERM workspace.

roles.title: Action or KRI responsible
roles.who: Who carries out a treatment action or measures an indicator.

tasks.text: See your pending actions and update their status
Record the value of your indicators when due
Warn when an action will not be done on time

roles.when: When an action is assigned and when a reminder arrives.

roles.title: Risk Committee or Board
roles.who: Who set the appetite and decide on the most important risks.

tasks.text: Approve the appetite and tolerance of each category
Formally accept the risks that will not be treated (never your own)
Approve the impact assessments of the AI systems
Analyse the quarterly report and the integrated map

roles.when: At every Committee meeting, with the quarterly report.

roles.title: Internal audit
roles.who: Third line: checks that the process works.

tasks.text: Consult the register, the reviews and the change history
Check current acceptances, segregation of duties and evidence
Download the methodology and the quarterly report as evidence

roles.when: According to the annual audit plan.

roles.title: AI officer
roles.who: Who keeps the inventory of AI systems and their assessments.

tasks.text: Register each AI system with its purpose, data and AI Act class
Carry out the impact assessment and submit it for approval
Create the corporate risk when the impact is significant

roles.when: Before putting an AI system into production and once a year.

roles.title: All staff

tasks.text: Report something that happened, almost happened or could happen
Follow the status of your reports in My reports

roles.when: Whenever you see a risk or an incident. Reporting in good faith is never penalized.

glossary.definition: Effect of uncertainty on objectives: something that could happen and would affect the organization.
glossary.example: Fraud with stolen identities in digital origination.

glossary.definition: What could happen, described in one sentence: what and to what.
glossary.example: "Outage of the telephony provider that stops customer service" (not "Providers").

glossary.definition: Why the event could happen.
glossary.example: Single provider without redundancy.

glossary.definition: What the event would cause if it happens.
glossary.example: Penalties for breaching the service level.

glossary.definition: How often it could happen in a year (scale 1 to 5).
glossary.example: 3 - Possible: once every 2 to 4 years.

glossary.definition: How serious it would be: money, customers, regulators, reputation and people (scale 1 to 5).
glossary.example: 4 - Major: regulatory sanction or loss of an important client.

glossary.definition: The risk if there were no controls at all.
glossary.example: Without identity validation, fraud would be likely and serious.

glossary.definition: What reduces probability or impact today: procedures, systems, approvals, insurance.
glossary.example: Biometric validation against the national registry.

glossary.definition: The risk considering the controls that work today. It is compared with the appetite.
glossary.example: With biometrics, fraud becomes unlikely.

glossary.definition: The level the treatment plan has to reach.
glossary.example: Go down from High to Medium before June.

glossary.definition: Level of risk the organization is willing to take in a category to achieve its objectives.
glossary.example: Fraud: Low appetite.

glossary.definition: Maximum admissible level; above it, immediate action is required.
glossary.example: Fraud: Medium tolerance.

glossary.definition: The decision on the risk: mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept.
glossary.example: Mitigate with an action plan.

glossary.definition: Committee decision to live with a risk, with a justification and for a period; never taken by the risk owner.
glossary.example: Accepted for 12 months because of the low exposure.

glossary.definition: Number that warns before the risk happens, with warning and critical thresholds.
glossary.example: Average days to collect: warning 60, critical 90.

glossary.definition: Something that actually happened: loss, near miss or unexpected gain. It is the evidence of the risk.
glossary.example: Loan granted with a forged ID: net loss 18,000,000.

glossary.definition: An event that happened but caused no loss.
glossary.example: Ransomware blocked by the antivirus.

glossary.definition: Periodic check of the risk that keeps a snapshot of the assessment as evidence.
glossary.example: Yearly review at the Committee.

glossary.definition: Person accountable for managing the risk, usually the manager of the process.
glossary.example: The credit manager for the delinquency risk.

glossary.definition: How much would be lost on average per year: frequency times average loss.
glossary.example: 1.3 events per year x 28 M = 37 M per year.

glossary.definition: Probability by impact matrix that shows where risks concentrate.
glossary.example: Critical risks are at the top right.

faq.q: I do not know which probability to choose. What do I do?
faq.a: Choose your best estimate and explain why in the description. If it already happened in recent years, it is at least Possible. Loss events and reviews will refine it.

faq.q: What is the difference between inherent and residual?
faq.a: Inherent is without controls; residual is with the controls that work today. The difference shows what the controls achieve.

faq.q: My risk is outside the appetite. Is it wrong?
faq.a: No: it means a decision is needed. Mitigate it with actions down to the target, or ask the Committee to accept it formally with a justification.

faq.q: Why can't I accept my own risk?
faq.a: Because of segregation of duties: who manages the risk cannot decide alone to live with it. The Committee accepts it.

faq.q: What do I do with the quality suggestions?
faq.a: Read them on the risk form and complete what is missing. They block nothing: they help keep the register consistent and auditable.

faq.q: How often must a risk be reviewed?
faq.a: At least once a year, and sooner if it is high or critical, if an event happens or if controls change.

faq.q: I do not receive the e-mail alerts.
faq.a: Notifications depend on the GLPI e-mail configuration. Ask the administrator.

faq.q: Where do I see what I have to do?
faq.a: In My ERM workspace: your pending actions, your indicators and your risks with their next review.
